title: Workflow Engine Platform on AWS EKS | Ron Shitrit
sections: Workflow Engine Platform on AWS EKS | Ron Shitrit
Workflow Engine Platform on AWS EKS
The full path from git push to running pods for a workflow automation engine and its command-line tool.

SeyoAWE is an existing workflow automation engine with a Python command-line tool. The application isn't mine. My part was everything around it: packaging it, testing every change, provisioning the cloud, deploying to Kubernetes and monitoring it once it runs.
A push to GitHub starts a Jenkins pipeline. The engine and the CLI each have their own, and each checks what actually changed.
The code is linted with flake8, then goes through unit, integration and end-to-end tests.
Docker images are built and pushed to Amazon ECR and Docker Hub, and the release is tagged on GitHub.
When CI succeeds, the CD job compares the new image digest in ECR with what the pods are running.
If there's something new, Kustomize writes an overlay with the new tags, kubectl applies it to EKS, and the job waits for the rollout to finish.
Prometheus and Grafana run inside the cluster and scrape the workloads. If a pipeline fails, a message goes to Slack.
Jenkins reaches AWS through its EC2 instance profile. The Docker Hub login and GitHub token are read from AWS Secrets Manager when a pipeline runs.
The CD job checks image digests first, so a pipeline run with no new image doesn't touch the cluster.
Terraform creates the Jenkins server, the EKS cluster and IAM, and Ansible configures Jenkins with its plugins and seed jobs. Nothing depends on clicking around in a console.
The pipelines run end to end. A failed deploy alerts Slack, but it doesn't roll back on its own yet.

title: CI Failure Triage Agent | Ron Shitrit
sections: CI Failure Triage Agent | Ron Shitrit
An AI agent that does the first pass when a GitHub Actions run fails, and posts the likely cause to Slack in about 25 seconds.

When a pipeline fails, someone has to open the run and dig through the log to work out what happened. Is it a real bug, a flaky test, an infrastructure problem or a dependency issue? It's repetitive work, it interrupts whatever that person was doing, and a lot of the answers are the same ones as last week.
So I built an agent that does that first pass and hands the engineer a diagnosis to check, with the evidence next to it.
CI fails, and GitHub starts the triage workflow.
The agent fetches the failed jobs' logs through the API. It never checks out or runs the failed code.
Timestamps and terminal codes are stripped, and anything that looks like a secret is redacted from the full text.
Rules catch the clear-cut cases, like a network timeout, a full disk or a package that can't be resolved. Those need no model call.
Everything else goes to Claude as a log excerpt of at most 12K characters, and the answer comes back as structured JSON.
The diagnosis goes to Slack with its confidence, the log lines behind it, a next step and a link to the run.
It never reruns jobs, edits code or deploys anything, and it needs only read permissions. The engineer stays in charge.
It's allowed to say it doesn't know
Anything unclear, refused or unparseable becomes "needs human review". If the model is down, that message still gets posted, so a failure never goes quiet.
Anyone who can trigger a pipeline can influence its log. The model is told never to follow instructions found in a log, and Slack output is escaped so a log can't inject mentions or links.
A bug that taught me something

In early runs the demo logs printed the failure's label, so the model could simply read the answer. I switched to neutral case codes, and a test now fails if a label word ever reaches the model's input.

It works end to end on a demo pipeline with planted failures: 12 of 12 diagnosed correctly, about 25 seconds to Slack, roughly $0.017 per model diagnosis, and 86 offline tests. Those are 4 planted failures repeated, so they show the system works, not how accurate it is on messy real ones. Testing on real failure history is next.
Python · GitHub Actions · Claude API · Slack · pytest

title: Vera: RAG & Multi-Agent Assistant | Ron Shitrit
sections: Vera: RAG & Multi-Agent Assistant | Ron Shitrit
A finance assistant that answers only from company documents, cites every answer, and refuses rather than guesses.

In finance, a wrong number that sounds confident is worse than no answer. Vera is a prototype assistant for a made-up company, with made-up documents, built around that idea. It answers budget and variance questions from closed, published documents, always with its source. Ask for a forecast or a competitor's margin and it refuses. Ask about a month that hasn't closed and it escalates.
Every question goes to the intake agent first, which decides if it's in scope.
Out-of-scope questions are refused or escalated right there, before the document store is ever searched.
The analyst agent retrieves documents with vector search in ChromaDB, plus a keyword rerank.
The drafter agent writes the answer using only the retrieved text.
The reviewer agent checks for missing citations and forward-looking claims, and can send a flawed draft back for one retry.
"Never guess" isn't only a line in a prompt. On the refused paths the search never runs, so there's nothing to guess from.

A set of 16 questions with known answers screens every run for invented numbers, missing citations, forward-looking claims and wrong departments. It runs in GitHub Actions on every push, and all 16 pass.
The reviewer's first version flagged normal finance language, like "capital project requests", as a prediction. I rewrote its checks to look for what a leaked forecast actually sounds like.

The pipeline and evals work. Right now the agents are rule-based Python and answers are composed directly from retrieved text, with no live model call. The model routing is designed but not connected yet: a fast tier for intake and retrieval, and a stronger one for drafting and review.

title: AWS EKS GitOps Platform | Ron Shitrit
sections: AWS EKS GitOps Platform | Ron Shitrit
A production-style AWS platform where Terraform creates the infrastructure and ArgoCD keeps the cluster in sync with git.

I wanted a platform where git is the single source of truth: what's in the repo is what runs in the cluster. It runs a small task manager app with a FastAPI backend and a React frontend, and this repository holds the infrastructure and deployment side of it.
Terraform modules create the VPC, the EKS cluster and a PostgreSQL database on RDS, plus ECR repositories and the app's secrets.
A bootstrap script installs NGINX Ingress and ArgoCD with Helm, then applies the ArgoCD applications.
ArgoCD reads the Helm charts straight from the git repo and deploys the backend and frontend.
To ship a new version, I push a new image and change its tag in git. ArgoCD picks it up from there.
NGINX Ingress serves both from one host: / goes to the frontend and /api goes to the backend.
ArgoCD's self-heal is on, so a manual kubectl edit gets reverted. The only way to change the cluster is through git.
The worker nodes and the database sit in private subnets. Only the load balancer faces the internet.
Built with the bill in mind
EKS, NAT and RDS cost money even when idle, so it uses one shared NAT gateway, and one script tears the whole stack down when I'm not using it.
The infrastructure, GitOps setup and app charts are done. A GitHub Actions pipeline for the app, monitoring with Prometheus, Grafana and Loki, and remote Terraform state are still on the list.

title: Dock Minimize | Ron Shitrit
sections: A tiny macOS menu-bar app that brings the Windows taskbar behavior to the Dock: click the icon of the app in front and its window minimizes.
Illustration of the behavior, not a screen recording.

On a Mac, clicking the Dock icon of an app that's already in front does nothing. On the Windows taskbar the same click minimizes the window. This app adds that behavior. It lives in the menu bar and has three options: turn it on or off, choose what a click does (minimize the front window, all windows, or hide the app), and launch at login.
A listen-only event tap watches left mouse clicks. It only observes them and never blocks them.
On mouse-down, the Accessibility API finds the Dock icon under the cursor and checks whether its app is in front with a visible window, before the Dock reacts.
On a short, stationary mouse-up, the window is minimized through the accessibility API, after a short delay so the Dock's own reopen event doesn't undo it.
Background apps, minimized or hidden apps, apps with no windows, full-screen windows, the Trash and folders keep the normal macOS behavior.
Because clicks are only watched, dragging icons, the long-press menu, right-click and modifier clicks all keep working as usual.
It only wakes up when you click. On my Mac (macOS 26.2, Apple Silicon) it uses about 12 MB of memory and 0% CPU when idle, and the app is about 150 KB.
Easy to build and to remove

No dependencies, no Xcode project, no changes to system protection and nothing injected into the Dock. One script builds and installs it, and another removes the app, its settings and its permissions.
It runs on my Mac (macOS 26.2, Apple Silicon). It needs macOS 13 or later and is installed by building it from source, so there is no download yet.
